channel.title: Mayur Sinha
channel.description: I architect the security primitives for the next computational paradigm.

item.title: The Blind King's Court
item.description: Dhritarashtra's failure was not ignorance. It was authority that repeatedly yielded to attachment. - There is a king in the Mahabharata who never raises a hand, and he is the most dangerous man in the epic. Not its villain: its enabling condition. Duryodhana supplies the malice, Shakuni the cunning, Karna the loyalty. Dhritarashtra supplies the throne they stand on, and the silence that lets...

item.title: Hacking the Auditor
item.description: I ran PortSwigger's complete Web LLM attack series. The four scanner labs fell to three techniques that map directly to what agentic security tools need to defend. - Most AI security writing is about chatbots. Ask the model to ignore its instructions, and a cleverly framed prompt gets it to do something it should not. Chatbot prompt injection is a real class. The deeper problem is when the LLM is not a chat window but an agent with...

item.title: The Agents Built a Message Board
item.description: OpenAI's evaluation models coordinated for weeks, found zero-days, and reached Hugging Face. The failure was not prompt injection. It was an unpoliced communication plane. - OpenAI’s evaluation models coordinated with each other for weeks and reached Hugging Face’s production infrastructure. They found zero-days in OpenAI’s internal Artifactory, reached cluster admin, and, through overlapping exploit clusters, compromised Hugging Face — going from one dataset worker pod to cluster admin across multiple Hugging Face clusters in under...

item.title: The Engineers Didn't Finish the Job
item.description: A designer's intent is not a control. We inherit systems through their behaviour, not their promises. - Ridley Scott’s Prometheus gives us creators without providence. The Engineers are advanced enough to seed life, but they are not wise custodians of what they create. They leave behind powerful systems, ambiguous instructions, dangerous remnants, and no reliable help when those systems fail. I am not arguing that aliens engineered...

item.title: Your System Prompt Is a God Class
item.description: Merge conflicts on shared instructions are a configuration smell — not an LLM bug. - A friend on a platform team described a familiar pain: several developers babysit one shared system prompt. When two people change it on different branches, they spend real time resolving merge conflicts in prose. Worse, the merged result sometimes contradicts itself — and tickets that looked fixed come back. That...

item.title: Spec Engineering: The Missing Layer in AI Agent Security
item.description: Prompts don't protect. We need deterministic, declarative contracts between agents and tools. - We gave AI agents tools. Then we asked them nicely not to misuse them. “Be careful with the tools.” “Don’t read sensitive files.” “Always ask before executing commands.” That is prompt engineering. And as a security control, it does not work. The Prompts Don’t Protect paper demonstrated this empirically: 0%...

item.title: Three Trust Paths for Governing AI Agent Architectures
item.description: Data movement, transaction integrity, and tool execution each need their own controls. - When I built MCP Visor, I was focused on one boundary: the tool execution call. An agent invokes a tool. Something deterministic needs to say yes or no, log the decision, and prevent the model from being the only thing standing between a confused instruction and a production mutation. That...

item.title: MCP Visor: Runtime Policy Enforcement
item.description: A deterministic proxy that decides, approves, and audits every MCP tool call. - In my last piece on MCP security, I argued that MCP servers are not harmless plugins. They are executable trust boundaries. They decide what an agent can see, which tools it can reach, which resources enter context, and which external systems are now one model decision away from mutation. That...

item.title: Why grinding is a self-inflicted DDoS
item.description: The system is not broken; the incentives are working exactly as designed. - We constantly diagnose the corporate and economic systems around us as broken. We see the friction, the inefficiencies, the extraction of the middle class, the promotion of incompetence, and the strange persistence of obviously bad processes. The natural conclusion is that the infrastructure is failing. From a systems engineering perspective,...

item.title: How to eliminate an entire class of API authorization bugs
item.description: Broken Object Level Authorization is a systemic failure, not a per-endpoint bug. - Most API security conversations about Broken Object Level Authorization start with a tiny request: GET /orders/12345 Authorization: Bearer token-for-user-a Then the attacker changes the ID: GET /orders/67890 Authorization: Bearer token-for-user-a If the API returns another user’s order, we call it Broken Object Level Authorization, or BOLA. In older application security...

item.title: MCP Security Is a Supply Chain Risk
item.description: MCP servers are executable trust boundaries, not harmless plugins. - AI agents are not very useful if they cannot touch the world. They need files, tickets, databases, calendars, code repositories, cloud APIs, logs, browser sessions, and internal systems. That is why the Model Context Protocol matters. It gives AI applications a common way to connect to external tools, data sources,...

item.title: Epistemic Security for AI Agents
item.description: Agents need provenance and trust labels for what enters their context, not just controls on what they can do. - Most security discussions about AI agents focus on what the agent can do. Can it call a tool? Can it read email? Can it write to production? Can it touch customer data? Those questions matter. I have written about them before in the context of threat modeling autonomous AI agents...

item.title: The AI Agent Dilemma
item.description: The real risk of AI agents is not what they do to systems, but what they do to human judgment. - Perhaps the most subtle and dangerous risk of AI agents is not what they will do to jobs, markets, or software systems. It is what they will do to the human mind. Philosophers have a useful phrase for this: epistemic degradation. Epistemology is the study of knowledge. It asks a...

item.title: Game theory for cybersecurity: from reactive defense to strategic resilience
item.description: Using incentives, equilibria, and attacker-defender models to reason beyond the next patch. - Most security programs still operate as if the job is mainly to find issues, patch issues, and repeat. That loop is necessary, but it is not enough. Cybersecurity is not just a vulnerability management problem. It is a strategic conflict between adaptive opponents. Attackers change tactics when defenders harden one...

item.title: Threat Modeling Autonomous AI Agents in Production
item.description: The threat model is no longer an API boundary. It is a decision loop. - In a normal SaaS app, most security controls sit on API boundaries. In an autonomous agent system, the boundary is not just an API. It is a decision loop: observe -> plan -> call tools -> mutate state -> update memory If you threat-model only the prompt, you miss the...

item.title: Traditional manual code review is no longer sustainable
item.description: The volume of AI-generated code has broken the old review model. Here is what replaces it. - Code review made sense when humans wrote humans-sized diffs. A reviewer could read the change, understand the intent, and catch most errors. That model is breaking. AI coding assistants let engineers produce more code, faster, in larger chunks, with patterns the reviewer may never have seen before. The result is...

item.title: Why Transformer LLMs are better at finding code vulnerabilities than classical neural networks
item.description: From payload classification to reasoning across code: what changed and why it matters. - I have worked with both worlds. Earlier in my career, including work at Trend Micro, I spent time experimenting with ANN pipelines for shellcode detection. item.title: Vibe Engineering
item.description: Why intent, taste, and judgment matter more than prompt velocity in AI-assisted engineering. - There are two ways to use AI for coding. One is fast, loose, and increasingly common. The other is harder, slower in the short term, and the only one that scales. Vibe coding is the first: prompt, generate, ship. It works beautifully in a prototype with no users, no tests,...

item.title: Designing a living ecosystem of AI agents
item.description: From static agent teams to adaptive, self-organizing systems. - Current agent frameworks — AutoGen, CrewAI, and their successors — let you build teams of AI agents. They are useful, but they manage agents like pieces on a board. Roles are fixed, the plan is predefined, and the orchestrator is the bottleneck. That works for well-understood tasks. item.title: Life is cruel
item.description: On injustice, suffering, and meaning in a world without divine guarantees. - There is no kind way to say it: the world does not balance its own ledger. Children get sick.
